clue.text: A slice of chorizo needed, as far as one can see

definitions.text: as far as one can see
definitions.note: a phrase describing the limit of sight, standing for the noun naming that limit

indicators.note: a slice is a thin cut from inside something, so the letters come from within the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the sausage name and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: A cook insists on a slice of spicy Spanish sausage, gesturing to show how much of it there is.
explanation.walkthrough: Chorizo is a spicy Spanish pork sausage; slicing off its first letter and running on into 'needed' gives HORIZON.
explanation.definitionFit: The horizon is the line where earth meets sky, the farthest limit of your vision in any direction.

clue.text: Neat hospital worker

blocks.note: first meaning: tidy, well arranged
second meaning: an attendant who does non-medical jobs on a ward

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like praise for a tidy nurse, but it is two separate meanings of one word: an adjective and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Tidy things are kept in good arrangement; separately, the noun names a ward attendant who moves patients and equipment.

clue.text: Originally introduced the aphorism 'love your country'

indicators.note: what comes originally comes at the start, so each following word supplies only its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letters of these five words

explanation.surface: Someone credits a famous saying about patriotism to the person who first coined it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'country' looks like part of the quoted saying, but it is the definition sitting outside the five words that do the work.
explanation.definitionFit: Italy is a nation in southern Europe, a straightforward example of the general category named.

clue.text: Make a comment that's awfully verbose

indicators.note: something done awfully is done badly, so the letters come out in a mangled order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone speaks up with a remark that rambles on far too long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awfully' looks like it intensifies 'verbose', but it is the signal to rearrange the very word it modifies.
explanation.definitionFit: To observe can mean to remark or state something, as in 'he observed that it was raining'.

clue.text: Baseball player's pet singer?

blocks.note: a common household pet
the American pop singer known by one name

explanation.surface: A question about which singer a baseball player keeps as a pet.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as possessive but stands for 'is'. Cher is the long-running American pop star.
explanation.definitionFit: The catcher is the fielder crouched behind home plate who receives the pitches thrown in baseball.

clue.text: Real and current

blocks.note: first meaning: genuine, existing in fact
second meaning: present, existing now

explanation.walkthrough: Two adjectives joined by 'and' look like a pair describing one thing; each is a separate meaning of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means existing in fact rather than imagined, and in older or legal use also means present or existing at this moment.

clue.text: Elaborate charade about time left for city feature

indicators.note: to elaborate is to work something up into a new form, so the letters are reworked
about means around, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: taken as written
T is the standard abbreviation for time
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A game of charades is staged with time left over for a city's main attraction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elaborate' could be a verb or adjective in the surface; here it rearranges all the letters. In Britain a city traditionally has a cathedral.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathedral is a major church and a typical landmark of a city; in Britain, having one historically conferred city status.

clue.text: Sounds like Hemingway is serious

indicators.note: sounding like something means matching it in speech, not in spelling

blocks.note: the first name of the American novelist Hemingway

explanation.surface: A remark that the famous novelist Hemingway comes across as a solemn man.
explanation.walkthrough: Ernest Hemingway's first name is pronounced the same as the adjective, echoing Wilde's play The Importance of Being Earnest.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnest describes someone sincere and intensely serious in manner, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Ties rocking horse's tail with pin

indicators.note: something rocking is moving to and fro, so the letters are shaken out of order

blocks.note: the possessive taken letter for letter
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone fastens ribbons to a rocking horse's tail with a pin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rocking horse' looks like a single toy, but 'rocking' is the signal working on the words after it, apostrophe-s included.
explanation.definitionFit: Ties are bonds or connections between people, which is what relationships are.

clue.text: Middleman's oddly abandoned notion

indicators.note: dropping the letters in odd positions leaves only those in even places

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A go-between has strangely given up on a plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' reads as 'strangely' but means the odd-numbered letters, which are the ones thrown away.
explanation.definitionFit: A notion is a thought or concept in the mind, a plain synonym of the answer.

clue.text: Top actress playing for them, say

definitions.note: the pronoun stands for the people a performer plays to

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are being toyed with and moved around

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A leading actress performs for an audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' reads as acting on stage, but it rearranges the two words before it; 'them, say' is the people being played for, with 'say' marking an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Those watching a performance are an audience of onlookers, the people a star actress plays for.

clue.text: The Lord has one for each letting in light

indicators.note: letting something in means admitting it inside, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: per means for each, as in 'per person'
a ray is a beam of light

explanation.surface: A church window lets light in, and every lord has one.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cryptic hint: the Lord's Prayer is the best-known Christian prayer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lord's Prayer, beginning 'Our Father', is a famous Christian prayer, so the Lord has one of these.

clue.text: Came to a vigil in the graveyard at last

indicators.note: at last means at the very end, so each word gives only its final letter

blocks.note: taken as written
a wake is a watch kept over the dead before burial
the final letters of these three words

explanation.surface: Mourners arrived for a night watch in a churchyard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Came to' looks like 'arrived at', but it means regained consciousness. A wake is a vigil over a body, fitting the graveyard scene.
explanation.definitionFit: To come to is to regain consciousness, and having woken up, you have been roused from sleep.

clue.text: [Extremely stormy night here: movement's not natural]

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outer letters of each word count

blocks.note: the first and last letters of each of these three words
a tic is an involuntary twitch of the muscles

explanation.surface: On a wild, stormy night, someone notices an eerie, unnatural motion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like it intensifies 'stormy', but it takes the two ends of each word. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Synthetic things are man-made or artificial, made by chemical process rather than occurring in nature.

clue.text: West End composer went ahead and took a trip

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: the final letter of this word
Maurice Ravel, the French composer of Bolero
to lead is to go in front

explanation.surface: A London theatre composer pressed on and went on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West End composer' suggests Andrew Lloyd Webber, but the West End is London's theatre district and here 'West' is split from its 'End'.
explanation.definitionFit: To travel is to go on a journey, so having taken a trip is the past tense of that verb.

clue.text: Setter values cross

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as I
to rate is to value or esteem

explanation.surface: A compiler's principles intersect, or the compiler values crossword clues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' sits at the end like a crossword reference, but it is the adjective meaning angry.
explanation.definitionFit: Cross, as an adjective, means annoyed or angry, which is exactly what irate describes.

clue.text: Devon and Cornwall listener's vow

blocks.note: these two English counties are in the South West, abbreviated SW
the ear is the organ you listen with

explanation.surface: A radio listener from the far west of England makes a solemn promise.
explanation.walkthrough: Devon and Cornwall are neighbouring counties at England's south-western tip. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To vow is to promise solemnly, and to swear an oath is to make exactly that kind of promise.

clue.text: If reporting rain or sunny spells, for example

indicators.note: a report is spoken out, so the word is taken as it is heard rather than spelt

blocks.clueFragment: rain or sunny spells, for example
blocks.note: rain and sunshine are examples of conditions in the atmosphere

explanation.surface: A forecaster asks whether to report rain or sunny periods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reporting' fits the weather forecast picture, but signals a sound-alike; 'If' is the definition, used as in 'ask if it will rain'.
explanation.definitionFit: In 'I wonder if it will rain', the conjunction can be swapped for its synonym introducing an indirect question.

clue.text: Emphasise policy must follow European articles

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the first-named piece is placed last

blocks.note: UN is a French article and DER a German one, both meaning 'a' or 'the'
a line is an official position, as in 'the party line'

explanation.surface: Someone stresses that a policy has to conform to European rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'articles' sounds like clauses of EU law, but means grammatical articles: French 'un' and German 'der'.
explanation.definitionFit: To underline a point is to stress or highlight it, figuratively drawing a line beneath it for emphasis.

clue.text: Appreciated conclusion about job yet unfinished

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps round the others
something unfinished lacks its ending, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: an end is a conclusion
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A worker valued finishing a task that is still incomplete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfinished' applies to both 'job' and 'yet', clipping each by its last letter before they go inside the conclusion.
explanation.definitionFit: To have appreciated something is to have taken pleasure in it, so the past tense of the verb fits.

clue.text: Sonatina played endlessly in many a country

definitions.note: the phrase is singular in form but means several countries, matching the plural

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is dropped
played suggests letters being performed freely in a different arrangement

blocks.note: the short sonata without its final letter

explanation.surface: A short piano piece is performed on and on all around the world.
explanation.walkthrough: A sonatina is a short, simple sonata. 'endlessly' looks like 'without stopping' but trims the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Nations are sovereign states, and 'many a country' is a roundabout way of saying lots of them.

clue.text: Her Majesty not disguising herself in rubber

blocks.note: ER is the royal cipher of Queen Elizabeth
someone not in disguise appears as themself
the Queen again, referring back

explanation.surface: The Queen goes undisguised while wearing rubber clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Someone not disguising herself appears as herself, so the Queen as the Queen gives the cipher, the little word, then the cipher again. In Britain a rubber is what Americans call an eraser.
explanation.definitionFit: In British English a rubber is the small block used to remove pencil marks, known elsewhere by this name.

clue.text: Look again for academic work

blocks.note: first meaning, split as RE plus SEARCH: hunt a second time
second meaning: systematic scholarly investigation

explanation.walkthrough: The first meaning is a split reading: 're-' means again and a search is a look, so a re-search is a second look.
explanation.definitionFit: Research is the systematic investigation scholars carry out; separately, read as re-search, it means to hunt through once more.

clue.text: Like shoulders of beef or lamb, they can be smoked

blocks.note: first meaning: large cuts of meat for roasting
second meaning: cannabis cigarettes

explanation.surface: A butcher's note that some cuts of meat can be cured over smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: Smoked meat fits the butcher's counter, but the second meaning is slang for rolled cannabis cigarettes.
explanation.definitionFit: A joint is a large cut of meat for roasting, and slang also for a hand-rolled cannabis cigarette.

clue.text: Intimate meal with no starter

indicators.note: a starter is the first course, so having none means losing the opening letter

blocks.note: the main evening meal

explanation.surface: A cosy dinner for two that skips the first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starter' plays on the first course of a meal, and on the first letter of a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Intimate thoughts are private and deeply personal, which is the sense of inner feelings or inner life.

clue.text: Pope endlessly fiddling with his holy principles

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is dropped
fiddling with something means tinkering with it, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the papal title without its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: The Pope keeps tinkering with his sacred doctrines.
explanation.walkthrough: The Pope and holy principles make a religious picture, but 'endlessly' and 'fiddling' are working on the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A philosophy can mean a set of guiding beliefs or principles by which someone lives.

clue.text: Almost nobody here at midday

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: nobody means no one

explanation.surface: A place that is nearly deserted at lunchtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost nobody' reads as 'hardly anyone'; it means the two-word phrase for nobody, minus its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Noon is twelve o'clock in the day, exactly the middle point, a straight synonym.

clue.text: Wrongfully arrest the first of dodgy dealers

indicators.note: something done wrongfully is done amiss, so the letters are put in the wrong order
the first of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: Police mistakenly detain the ringleader of some shady dealers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrongfully arrest' reads as a miscarriage of justice, but 'Wrongfully' is rearranging the word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dealers are people who buy and sell goods, and traders are exactly that, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Location of a debutante's first gown

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter only

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of this word
a gown is a long formal dress

explanation.surface: Where a young society woman's first ball gown can be found.
explanation.walkthrough: A debutante is a young woman formally presented to society, traditionally in a white gown.
explanation.definitionFit: An address is the details of where someone lives or a building stands, so it names a location.
